opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that "picking up and reproducing patterns" is actually a lot more powerful than people give it credit for. That's what a great deal of human culture is. When I read a book or go to a library, I'm getting access to the patterns that other people have discovered. So my view has been that these large models are best thought of as cultural technologies, like writing, or print, or libraries, or search engines. They're extraordinarily good ways of summarizing and passing on what other humans have already figured out. And that's not a small thing. Print transformed the world.

But what would impress me as something different in kind? What I'd want to see is the thing that every two-year-old does, and that's going out into the world, doing experiments, and discovering something genuinely new about how the world works, something that wasn't already there in the data. In my lab we give kids these little machines, the "blicket detectors," where some blocks make the machine light up and play music and some don't. Even very young children will figure out the causal structure. And crucially, they'll do things to find out. They'll try putting the blocks on in different combinations. They're curious, they explore, they do things that look kind of crazy and random from the outside, but they're actually extremely effective ways of finding out about causal structure.

When we've tested the large models on those same kinds of tasks, they do quite well when the answer is the conventional one, the one that's in the text. But when the right answer is the unusual one, when you have to override what you've heard before because the evidence in front of you says something different, the children, even four-year-olds, are much better at that than the models.

So the evidence that would really impress me would be a system that, faced with a new environment, actively goes out and explores, that is intrinsically motivated to find out, that designs its own experiments, and that ends up with a causal model it didn't have before and couldn't have got just by summarizing what humans had already written down. Something like the scientist in the crib, if you like. And I think the interesting thing is that's not just a matter of scaling up. It's a different kind of problem. It's the explore side of the explore-exploit trade-off, and childhood is the evolutionary solution to that problem. We have this long, protected period where we get to explore without having to worry about exploiting. The models are basically all exploit, no childhood.

r001.rationale: The response says an impressive system would design its own experiments in a new environment and discover a causal model it could not have obtained by summarizing what humans had written down.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that I think the framing of "just patterns" versus "real reasoning" is a bit of a false dichotomy, and it's one that's gotten us into trouble on both sides. A lot of what human beings do, including a lot of what we'd call thinking, is picking up and reproducing patterns. So I don't want to set up a test where the AI fails simply because it's doing something humans also do.

What I actually care about, and what I've spent forty years looking at in children, is something more specific. It's the ability to go out and get new information about the world when the information you have isn't good enough. A two-year-old doesn't just consume the data that happens to be in front of her. She notices that something doesn't fit, she forms a hypothesis, and then she does something, she pokes the thing, she drops it, she asks "why?" for the fortieth time, and she revises what she believes based on what comes back. The loop runs through the world, not just through the text.

So what would impress me is this. Give one of these systems a problem where the answer genuinely isn't in the training distribution, where the causal structure is novel, and where the only way to figure it out is to intervene, run the right experiment, look at the result, and update. Not a puzzle that has a clever solution hiding in the corpus somewhere, but a situation where the model would have to say, "I don't know, and here is what I would have to do to find out," and then actually be good at choosing that action. Children are remarkably good at this. They're better than adults in some respects, because they're less committed to their priors.

The second thing I'd look for is whether the system knows what it doesn't know in a way that's calibrated to the world rather than to the plausibility of the sentence. When a four-year-old doesn't know something, she's uncertain about the world. When a language model is uncertain, as far as I can tell, it's uncertain about what the next word should be. Those can look alike on the surface and be completely different underneath.

And I'll add one more thing, which is slightly against myself. I've been struck that these reasoning models are better at some of these tasks than I expected a few years ago. I was fairly confident the gap would be larger. So I try to hold the hypothesis loosely. But I still think the fundamental difference is that we're learning from a world that pushes back, and they're learning from what we said about it. Until that changes, I think "cultural technology" rather than "agent" is the right description, and it's not a diminishing one. Writing and printing are cultural technologies too, and they changed everything.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI should intervene, run experiments, and update on a novel causal problem. It does not say the experiments must reveal something previously unknown to the people around the system.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think “picking up patterns” is doing a lot of work in that question. We pick up patterns, too. The interesting question is what you can do with what you’ve learned when you encounter something genuinely new.

What would impress me is a system that could go into an unfamiliar environment, figure out which questions to ask, and perform experiments that distinguish between different explanations. Suppose it thinks that one thing causes another. Can it devise an intervention, discover that its idea was wrong, and come up with a better idea? And can it do that without someone having already structured the problem and supplied the relevant possibilities?

That’s something children do remarkably well. They don’t just answer the questions we give them. They explore, and their exploration changes what they understand. I’d find that sort of autonomous discovery much more compelling than getting a very high score on a set of reasoning problems. It wouldn’t establish that the system wasn’t learning patterns. It would establish that it could use learning to discover something about the world.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI autonomously designing experiments and discovering things about the world, but it does not say those discoveries were previously unknown to people around the system.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I’d want to be careful about that distinction, because picking up patterns can mean almost anything. We pick up patterns, too. The interesting question is what kinds of representations you’re building and what you can do with them.

What would impress me is a system that could encounter a genuinely unfamiliar environment, come up with hypotheses about how it works, and then choose actions that would distinguish those hypotheses. Not just get the right answer, but figure out what experiment to do when it doesn’t know the answer—and revise its ideas when the experiment comes out differently than it expected.

That’s something young children do remarkably well. They don’t just learn from the data that happen to be presented to them. They go out and get the data. So I’d be particularly interested in evidence of that kind of flexible, self-directed causal learning, especially in situations where the system couldn’t simply have encountered lots of similar problems in its training.

r001.rationale: The response describes models generating hypotheses and choosing experiments to distinguish them in unfamiliar settings, but does not say those experiments reveal something previously unknown to people around them.
